params.question: Which combination of clinical features should raise suspicion that a patient's skin condition is HIV-related?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features suggest a photodermatosis or contact dermatitis. HIV-related dermatoses are characterised by how the lesions behave — spreading extensively, looking atypical, and resisting standard treatment.

answers.text: Extensive, atypical, and refractory to standard treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HIV weakens the immune system, causing familiar skin conditions to become more widespread than expected, present with unusual morphology or distribution, and respond poorly to conventional treatment.
Localised, self-limiting disease is the opposite of what HIV produces. HIV-related dermatoses tend to spread widely across multiple sites and persist despite adequate treatment.

answers.text: Acute, febrile, and associated with generalised lymphadenopathy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While fever and lymphadenopathy may accompany HIV systemically, the three specific hallmarks of HIV-related skin disease refer to how the lesions themselves behave: extensive spread, atypical presentation, and treatment resistance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three red flags are extensive, atypical, and refractory. Think of seborrhoeic dermatitis covering the chest and back instead of just the scalp, or herpes zoster crossing multiple dermatomes — familiar diseases made unfamiliar by immunosuppression.
Exactly right. Whenever you see a skin condition that is more widespread, more unusual in appearance, or more resistant to treatment than you'd expect, consider HIV as the underlying driver.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with white, corrugated plaques on th

params.question: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with white, corrugated plaques on the lateral border of the tongue that cannot be scraped off. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Candidal thrush produces removable white plaques — when scraped, the underlying mucosa appears erythematous. This patient's plaques are non-removable, which points to a different aetiology.
Oral lichen planus typically produces a lacy, reticular pattern (Wickham striae) on the buccal mucosa rather than corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue.

Correct. Oral hairy leukoplakia, driven by Epstein-Barr virus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients, produces white corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue that characteristically cannot be scraped off — unlike candidal thrush.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma can present as a white lesion, but it typically forms an indurated, ulcerated mass rather than the bilateral corrugated plaques characteristic of EBV-driven oral hairy leukoplakia.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinguishing feature is removability. Candidal thrush can be scraped off (and is KOH-positive), while oral hairy leukoplakia — driven by EBV — produces corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be removed.
Well done. The non-removable corrugated plaque on the lateral tongue is the clinical signature of oral hairy leukoplakia — a key mucocutaneous clue to HIV-associated immunosuppression.

interactions.label: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with violaceous

params.question: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with violaceous nodules on the lower extremities. Which investigation definitively distinguishes Kaposi sarcoma from bacillary angiomatosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The CD4 count confirms the depth of immunosuppression but cannot differentiate between vascular-appearing lesions. Both Kaposi sarcoma and bacillary angiomatosis occur at low CD4 counts.
The KOH preparation identifies fungal elements — pseudohyphae for Candida, septate hyphae for dermatophytes. It has no role in differentiating vascular or violaceous skin lesions.
The Tzanck smear demonstrates multinucleated giant cells in herpesvirus infections (HSV, VZV). It is not relevant to the work-up of violaceous nodules.

Correct. Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8 driven malignancy), bacillary angiomatosis (curable Bartonella infection), and pyogenic granuloma can look nearly identical clinically. Histopathology is definitive — and the distinction matters enormously because bacillary angiomatosis responds to antibiotics.

overallFeedback.feedback: The definitive investigation is skin biopsy with histopathology. Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and pyogenic granuloma can look clinically identical, yet their management differs dramatically — BA is curable with antibiotics, making histological confirmation essential.

Exactly. When violaceous or vascular lesions appear at low CD4 counts, clinical appearance alone is unreliable. Biopsy separates a curable infection from a malignancy — a distinction that directly changes management.

interactions.label: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is a form of drug allergy to

params.question: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is a form of drug allergy to antiretroviral medications and requires immediate cessation of ART.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: IRIS is not a drug allergy at all. It represents a flare of a pre-existing infection triggered by immune reconstitution after starting ART. Unlike Stevens-Johnson syndrome or DRESS, IRIS does not require cessation of antiretroviral therapy — stopping ART would be counterproductive.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. IRIS is not a drug allergy. It occurs when the recovering immune system mounts an inflammatory response against pre-existing infections such as herpes zoster, molluscum, or mycobacterial disease. Unlike true drug reactions such as SJS/TEN, IRIS does not require stopping antiretroviral therapy.

interactions.label: Before starting a patient on abacavir-based ART, which genetic test must be perf

params.question: Before starting a patient on abacavir-based ART, which genetic test must be performed to prevent a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HLA-B*27 is associated with spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis. It has no relevance to abacavir prescribing safety.

Correct. Patients carrying the HLA-B*57:01 allele are at high risk of systemic abacavir hypersensitivity — fever, rash, and gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms. Re-challenge after such a reaction can be fatal, making pre-prescription screening mandatory.
G6PD deficiency screening is important before prescribing drugs like dapsone or primaquine to prevent haemolytic anaemia. The pharmacogenomic test relevant to abacavir safety is HLA-B*57:01.
CYP2B6 polymorphisms affect efavirenz metabolism and its neuropsychiatric side effects. The genetic marker linked to fatal abacavir hypersensitivity is the HLA-B*57:01 allele.

overallFeedback.feedback: HLA-B*57:01 is the correct test. Patients carrying this allele develop systemic hypersensitivity to abacavir with fever, rash, and multi-organ involvement. Re-challenge can be fatal — making pre-prescription genetic screening essential.
Exactly right. HLA-B*57:01 screening before starting abacavir is a textbook example of pharmacogenomics preventing a fatal adverse reaction. A positive result means abacavir must never be prescribed.

interactions.label: A patient on nevirapine-based ART develops painful, widespread skin detachment a

params.question: A patient on nevirapine-based ART develops painful, widespread skin detachment affecting 18% of body surface area with mucosal erosions. How is this reaction classified?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SJS is defined by epidermal detachment affecting less than 10% of body surface area. At 18% BSA involvement, the reaction has progressed beyond this threshold.

Correct. The SJS–TEN spectrum is classified purely by BSA of epidermal detachment: SJS (<10%), SJS–TEN overlap (10–30%), and TEN (>30%). At 18%, this falls in the overlap zone. The offending drug must be stopped immediately and urgent supportive care initiated.
TEN is classified as epidermal detachment exceeding 30% of body surface area. At 18% BSA, this reaction falls in the SJS–TEN overlap zone (10–30%), not yet TEN.

DRESS presents with fever, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement — typically 2–8 weeks after drug exposure. The hallmark of the SJS–TEN spectrum is widespread epidermal detachment, classified by the percentage of BSA affected.

overallFeedback.feedback: The SJS–TEN spectrum is a continuum classified by the percentage of body surface area showing epidermal detachment: SJS (<10%), SJS–TEN overlap (10–30%), and TEN (>30%). At 18%, this is SJS–TEN overlap — and the offending drug must be stopped immediately.

Well done. Knowing the BSA thresholds — under 10% for SJS, 10 to 30% for overlap, over 30% for TEN — lets you grade severity accurately, which directly guides the urgency and level of supportive care required.
